_note: Only one credible naked-eye-class prospect (mag ~6 or brighter) was found for late 2026–2027, and even it is a severe twilight target. 1P/Halley is the exception: included for its 2061 return, the one long-range comet arrival that is a certainty rather than a prospect. Per the project rules, no fainter comets were padded in and no dates were guessed. Newly discovered comets can always outburst, so this list should be re-checked closer to 2027.
_source: J. D. Shanklin — Comet prospects for 2027 (people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~jds/preds27.pdf)
Orbital elements for 2P/Encke: Minor Planet Center, epoch 2026 Oct 18 (q, e, i, node, argPeri, time of perihelion as Julian date) — used only for approximate where-to-look positions
Orbital elements for 1P/Halley: Minor Planet Center (MPC 191592), epoch 2026 Oct 23 (q, e, i, node, argPeri, time of perihelion as Julian date) — used only for approximate where-to-look positions
2061 return of 1P/Halley: perihelion 28 July 2061 and predicted peak apparent magnitude about −0.3 (vs +2.1 in 1986), as published in the standard references for the return

events.name: 2P/Encke
events.note: Bright on paper but nearly unobservable: peak brightness occurs only about 10° from the Sun, so this is an expert twilight target at best, not a practical backyard comet.

events.name: 1P/Halley
events.note: The famous one, back after 75 years — and this return is the good kind: unlike 1986, when it was on the far side of the Sun, in 2061 it is on Earth's side at perihelion and closest to Earth a day later, so published predictions put the peak around magnitude −0.3 (some say nearer 0) — an easy naked-eye comet. At perihelion it sits only ~25° from the Sun, a pre-dawn twilight target; through August it pulls away to ~40° and becomes an early-evening object. Positions here come from two-body Kepler motion with no planetary perturbations, so treat them as where-to-look guidance, not an ephemeris.
events.source: Minor Planet Center elements (MPC 191592), epoch 2026 Oct 23; 2061 return predictions
